intro: Schubert’s Unfinished begins with cellos and basses alone, then lets oboe and clarinet sing over murmuring violins. Leopold Stokowski conducts the Philadelphia Orchestra in this 1927 recording of its first movement.

sections.label: A · Low strings, then two singing woodwinds
sections.mNote: B minor opens into the cellos’ G-major melody

sections.label: Dev · The low-string theme grows in E minor
sections.mNote: The opening phrase climbs towards a trombone-led climax

sections.label: A′ · Oboe and clarinet return
sections.mNote: The violin murmur returns beneath the two woodwinds

sections.label: Coda · The low strings return in B minor
sections.mNote: The opening phrase leads towards the final chords

cues.title: Cellos and basses alone
cues.text: Eight bars for cellos and basses, pianissimo. Their dark B-minor phrase is the symphony’s first voice. The violins then begin their restless murmur, and oboe and clarinet sing together above it.
cues.evidence: Schubert’s Werke, Series I, No. 8 (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1885), first movement, pp. 1–2. The opening and scoring are also described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The cellos sing in G
cues.text: After a brief horn-led bridge, the cellos begin a long melody in G major. The violins take it up over gently off-beat accompaniment. A tune this welcoming seems to promise a very different symphony.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1885), first movement, bars 38–41 and the following second subject; melody, key and syncopated accompaniment described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chords cut through the song
cues.text: Heavy chords from the full orchestra interrupt the G-major melody. Schubert leaves silences between the blows, then takes fragments of the tune through the closing passage. The singing line has become an argument.
cues.evidence: First movement, exposition closing group: tutti sforzandi, pauses and variants of the G-major theme. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The opening phrase in E
cues.text: The development starts quietly in E minor with the phrase that opened the symphony. The low strings bring it back, and the higher strings take it up. What first sounded like an introduction now supplies the movement’s central struggle.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1885), first movement, p. 7; the E-minor development of the introductory theme is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The trombones take over
cues.text: The trombones turn the opening phrase into a forceful declaration above the orchestra. E minor holds through the long climax. The tune once entrusted to the lowest strings has acquired a brass voice.
cues.evidence: First movement, development climax: prominent trombone variant of the introductory theme in E minor. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Vienna hears it in 1865
cues.text: On 17 December 1865 Johann von Herbeck conducts the first performance in Vienna, forty-three years after Schubert begins the score. He follows its two completed movements with the busy D-major finale of Schubert’s Third Symphony.
cues.evidence: Première date, conductor and appended finale: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert), Early history.

cues.title: Two woodwinds come home
cues.text: Oboe and clarinet return over the violins’ murmur. Schubert brings back their melody quietly in B minor, leaving out the eight-bar introduction. The two woodwinds sound almost private after the trombones.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1885), first movement, pp. 11–12: end of development and recapitulation. https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.8,_D.759_(Schubert,_Franz)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The cello tune in D
cues.text: The cello melody returns in D major, a fourth below its first appearance in G. The tune keeps its easy swing, but its new key brings it closer to the surrounding B minor.
cues.evidence: First movement, second subject in the recapitulation, transposed from G major to D major. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back to the low strings
cues.text: After the recapitulation reaches B major, the coda restores B minor and the low-string opening. Schubert makes the once-whispered phrase lead the final confrontation, ending with emphatic orchestral chords.
cues.evidence: First movement, B-major close of the recapitulation and B-minor coda based on the introductory theme. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A B pedal, then E minor
transitions.from: A · Low strings, then two singing woodwinds
transitions.to: Dev · The low-string theme grows in E minor
transitions.how: The exposition holds B in the second bassoon and first horn beneath an F♯-major chord. The development then begins softly in E minor: cellos and basses recover the opening phrase, and the higher strings take it up.
transitions.evidence: First movement, bar 109 and the opening of the development; Breitkopf & Härtel score (1885), p. 7. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)

transitions.title: The violin murmur returns
transitions.from: Dev · The low-string theme grows in E minor
transitions.how: The orchestral outburst recedes into soft flute and oboe phrases. Oboe and clarinet then recover the B-minor melody over murmuring violins and plucked lower strings. The eight-bar introduction is omitted.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1885), first movement, pp. 11–12. https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.8,_D.759_(Schubert,_Franz)

transitions.title: B major darkens to minor
transitions.to: Coda · The low strings return in B minor
transitions.how: B major closes the recapitulation. The coda changes it to B minor and restores the opening phrase in the low strings. Its return begins the final build towards the orchestra’s closing chords.
transitions.evidence: First movement, end of recapitulation and coda. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)

source.title: Schubert, Symphonie in H moll (unvollendet), Schubert’s Werke, Serie 1 Nr. 8 (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1885)
source.locator: IMSLP #73284, first movement, Allegro moderato, printed pages 1–18.

timeline.note: Cellos and basses begin alone, pianissimo, in B minor.
Violins murmur above plucked violas, cellos and basses.
Oboe and clarinet sing in unison over the murmuring violins.
Four bars of horns and bassoons prepare G major.
Cellos, then violins, sing the G-major tune over off-beat strings.
The full orchestra strikes sforzando chords, with silences between them.
Cellos and basses recover the opening phrase quietly in E minor; the upper strings take it up.
Trombones proclaim the opening phrase over the full orchestra.
Flutes and oboes carry the quiet phrases that close the development.
Oboe and clarinet return above the violins’ B-minor murmur.
The low strings recall the opening phrase as the coda begins.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition and any cuts or retouchings by the conductor are not identified in the sources consulted.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Bolig dates all three sides of the first movement (CVE-29052, -29053 and -29054) to 28 April 1927. The Internet Archive description and Pristine give the two session days (28 and 30 April 1927) for the symphony as a whole.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Academy of Music, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Stokowski’s earlier acoustic recording of 1924 used the same matrix numbers without the CVE prefix and different issue numbers (Bolig lists 74894–74897 and 6459–6460); this transfer is the electrical recording of 1927 by its description, session dates and Victor numbers.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The Internet Archive description says “Originally issued as Victor 6663, 6664 & 6665. (Later as a set as M-16.)”; Pristine gives the same numbers and album. Bolig also lists later Victor and HMV issues of the same sides. The disc and side on which the movement boundary falls are not identified; the allocation of matrices to movements follows Bolig’s part numbers.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Parts 1–3: CVE-29052, take 6; CVE-29053, take 6; CVE-29054, take 6
fields.note: Bolig and the Pristine producer’s note agree on the matrices and takes of the first movement. The DAHR matrix pages could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error). No run-out inspection has been made of the digital surrogate.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The Internet Archive description reads “Transfer by Bob Varney”.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was added on 24 January 2011, which is an upload date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: The stylus, equalisation, speed and noise treatment are not documented. The file runs 10:28; Pristine’s own restoration runs 10:33, so the two transfers differ by a few seconds, and where the side joins fall in this file is not known.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Schubert died in 1828. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: The Internet Archive item carries a CC0 licence URL declared by the uploader, which is not treated as authority to waive Victor’s rights. The pre-1963 European rule applies because the recording was made in 1927 and was on sale by January 1928 (a Victor advertisement in The Golden Book Magazine offers Records Nos. 6663-4-5), so the 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension; the exact first issue date is not established. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence. The recording was published after 1925, so a US public-domain basis is not established.
alts: Pre-1963 European public domain — territorial basis.
CC0 — licence URL on the Internet Archive item, uploader’s declaration.

composer.epithet: At seventeen he set a spinning wheel turning under Gretchen’s voice; at thirty-one he could make two cellos sing as if they had always belonged together.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition lessons with Antonio Salieri
School assistant; tutor to the Esterházy daughters at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; independent composer
The singer Vogl, the poets Schober and Mayrhofer, the painter Schwind, Josef von Spaun
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and stage works

quote.text: I like these songs more than all the others, and you will come to like them too.
quote.source: Schubert to his friends about Winterreise, 1827, as Josef von Spaun later recalled; our translation

composer.background:
In the Schubert family quartet, Franz played the viola. His brothers took the violins and his father the cello: the future songwriter learnt to make himself heard from an inner part. He was born on 31 January 1797 in Himmelpfortgrund, a Viennese suburb, and grew up in his father’s schoolhouse. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer helped with the rest. At eleven he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school, where the orchestra put Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven under his fingers.

Salieri began teaching him composition in 1812. The next year Schubert left the boarding school, trained as a teacher and returned to his father’s classroom as an assistant. On 19 October 1814, aged seventeen, he wrote Gretchen am Spinnrade. The piano’s right hand turns the wheel, the left hand works the treadle, and Goethe’s girl cannot stop thinking about Faust. At the remembered kiss the mechanism stops. The following year brought roughly 140 songs, among them Erlkönig, as well as church music, a symphony and works for the stage.
